title: Evaluating LLM applications before they ship
summary: How do you know an LLM system is ready for production? An open evaluation suite for retrieval, tool use, and safety that compares models and designs on quality, failures, latency, and cost.

buildsOn.text: the RAG and tool-using systems I’ve shipped, where access control, audit logging, and release evaluation were requirements.

approach: Three workloads on one fictional company: question answering over its documents (RAG), multi-step tasks using tools and a SQL database, and adversarial cases (prompt injection, out-of-scope requests, and other users’ data).
About 50 hand-written cases per workload, with reference answers, kept separate from anything used to tune prompts.
Two designs compared: rules written in the prompt, and checks enforced in code (retrieval filters, permission-checked tools, output validation).
Run across Claude, GPT, Gemini, and one open model served locally, 3 runs each.
measures: Answer correctness, and whether each answer is supported by the retrieved text
Tool-task success and policy violations, read from logs instead of judged by an LLM
How closely the LLM judge agrees with my own labels on a sample
p50 / p95 latency and cost per request
publishes: Public repo that reproduces every number with one command

title: Fine-tuning and serving small open models
summary: When does a fine-tuned small open model beat prompting a frontier API? Measured on quality, latency, and cost, on one 24 GB GPU.

buildsOn.text: my production fine-tuning work: SFT and LoRA for open-source LLMs, contrastive embedding models, and transformer classifiers taken from 78% to 89% accuracy.

approach: Three task types where teams usually prompt a frontier API: structured extraction to JSON, tool calling, and classification.
LoRA and QLoRA fine-tuning of Qwen, Llama, and Gemma models in the 4–12B range, with held-out test sets that are never used for training.
Served with vLLM as LoRA adapters, in BF16, and quantized (AWQ, plus GPTQ or FP8), then load-tested at 1 to 32 concurrent users.
A general-skills check before and after fine-tuning, to catch regressions.
measures: Task accuracy against a frontier API on the same test sets
How much training data each task needs
Time to first token, p95 latency, and throughput
Cost per 1,000 requests, with the assumptions stated
publishes: Adapters with model cards on Hugging Face

title: Reinforcement learning for reasoning and instruction following
summary: Can reinforcement learning (GRPO) make a small open model reason and follow instructions better than supervised fine-tuning alone, and how does the model learn to game the reward?

buildsOn.text: my production fine-tuning work: SFT and LoRA training pipelines with evaluation built in, taken one step further from supervised learning to reinforcement learning.

approach: Two general skills where a program can check the answer: math reasoning (reward for the correct final answer) and following instructions with checkable rules such as length limits, required formats, and keywords.
A 3–4B open instruct model trained with GRPO and LoRA, compared against the prompted base model and supervised fine-tuning alone, across 3 seeds.
Scored on standard held-out test sets (GSM8K test, MATH-500, and IFEval) that are never used for training.
Runs on one 24 GB GPU, with vLLM generating the training samples.
measures: Benchmark accuracy for each method, with confidence intervals
A general-skills check, to see whether gains on one skill cost another
Reward curves, answer length, and training cost compared with supervised fine-tuning
Reward hacking: what the model learned that earned reward without being right, and how it was closed
